archetype.name: Game Manager (veteran backup)
archetype.definition: A 33-year-old undrafted veteran whose job is to keep a run-first offense on schedule with short, on-time throws, and who has never had the arm or accuracy to carry a game when that plan breaks down.

report.headline: Two September games went badly wrong; now he's the Falcons' third quarterback, not their answer.
report.take:
Cooper Rush's 2026 is two games long and it's over unless something goes wrong ahead of him. He started Week 1 at Pittsburgh, came on for Tua Tagovailoa in Week 2 against Carolina, and has not taken a meaningful snap since. Michael Penix Jr. started Weeks 3 through 10, and the depth chart lists Rush as QB3. Read every number below as the record of two bad afternoons from an emergency option, not a running verdict on a starter.

The afternoons were bad. His -0.513 EPA per dropback ranks 52nd of 55 qualifiers, his CPOE of -13.61 ranks 53rd, and he threw four interceptions on 39 attempts, a 10.3% rate against a league average of 2.5%. The shape of it is what stands out. He threw almost entirely underneath, with 5.34 intended air yards and an average throw landing about five yards short of the sticks. Bijan Robinson drew 14 of his targets, and on those quick throws he was merely below average. The damage came when he pushed the ball. Three of the four picks came on seven intermediate attempts, a bucket that cost -9.5 EPA on its own, and throws over the middle went 37.5% complete with two interceptions.

The tape doesn't support blaming the line. Atlanta's offense allows the fewest QB hits in the league, yet 62.5% of his pressures became sacks and 15.9% of his dropbacks ended with him hit or sacked. That sack rate is probably noise: his career pressure-to-sack marks ranked 4th in 2022 and 2nd in 2025, so getting the ball out has always been his best trait. The accuracy is the real flaw. His CPOE has been negative every season of his career, and this year's drop of 11.7 points from 2025 is the extreme end of a trait he has always had. His bad-throw rate also jumped from 17.3% to 23.1%.

Where it's heading is simple. He is insurance behind Penix and whoever sits at QB2, and the only way he sees the field is through injuries or a blowout. If he does play, expect what he has always been: a quick-game passer who looks competent throwing to the left and under center (small samples) and who struggles when a defense takes away the checkdown and makes him throw between the hashes.

strengths.title: Gets the ball out quickly
strengths.body: For his whole career Rush has avoided sacks by throwing on time. His pressure-to-sack rate ranked 4th in 2022 and 2nd in 2025. This year's 62.5% comes from a handful of pressures in two games, one of them a 34-point loss, so trust the multi-year trait over the two-game number.

strengths.title: Functional in the quick game
strengths.body: On throws under 10 air yards he completed 63.3%, and attempts to the left side produced +0.338 EPA. That isn't good, but it is playable, and it is the version of Rush an offense can win with in spot duty. Five under-center snaps went +0.953 EPA, which hints that play-action and a structured run game suit him, though five plays prove nothing on their own.

concerns.title: Accuracy collapses past the sticks
concerns.body: Throws of 10 or more air yards went 33.3% complete with three interceptions and -1.137 EPA per play. This is an extension of a career-long weakness: his CPOE has been negative every season. He was more careless this year, with intermediate and middle-of-the-field throws producing most of the damage.

concerns.title: Can't move the chains on third down
concerns.body: He converted 15.4% of his third downs, facing an average of 8.5 yards to go, with a -36.1 CPOE. A passer who aims short of the sticks by design needs manageable distances. Once the down and distance get long he has no answer, which is how a game-manager profile turns into a liability.

concerns.title: Third string on the depth chart
concerns.body: Penix has started eight straight games, and Rush is listed as QB3. His fantasy and real-world value now depends entirely on injuries ahead of him, and even a relief appearance would come with little practice work with the starters.

trend.note: Week 2 was worse than Week 1: CPOE fell from -10.4 to -16.8 and the bad-throw rate rose from 19% to 29.4%, plus a lost fumble. He then dropped out of the rotation entirely behind Penix.

nextGame.headline: Unlikely to play, and Minnesota is the worst possible draw if he does
nextGame.body:
Rush is QB3, so the realistic expectation for Week 12 is zero snaps. If injuries forced him in, Minnesota is the hardest matchup on the schedule for his profile. The Vikings rank 1st in pass defense EPA, 1st in sack rate and 1st in QB hit rate, and allow the fewest fantasy points a game to quarterbacks. They also let up few explosive passes, which squeezes the underneath game Rush depends on. Opponents run against them more than any defense in the league, though, so the Falcons would likely lean on the ground game and limit his volume.

Minnesota will be without CB Isaiah Rodgers, an 83%-snap starter, which helps whoever is throwing to Drake London. Their WR1 matchup has also been leaky on a per-target basis. On the other side, Kyler Murray and Jordan Addison are both out, which keeps the Vikings' 30th-ranked offense from forcing a shootout. With Atlanta a 7-point road underdog and a 42.5 total, a low-scoring, run-leaning game is the likeliest script.

keyMatchups.title: Pass rush vs a sack-prone fill-in
keyMatchups.body: Minnesota leads the league in both sack rate and hit rate. Rush turned 62.5% of his pressures into sacks this season, even if his career record says that number should come down. This is the matchup most likely to make a relief appearance go badly.

keyMatchups.title: London against a short-handed secondary
keyMatchups.body: London was the one target Rush produced with, at +0.334 EPA per target. Minnesota ranks 27th in EPA allowed to opposing WR1s and is missing Rodgers. If Atlanta's passing game does anything, it probably runs through London.

keyMatchups.title: Run funnel caps pass volume
keyMatchups.body: Offenses run against Minnesota more than against any other defense. Atlanta already passes less than situation predicts (29th in pass rate over expected), so the game plan would protect any backup quarterback.

nextGame.watch: Whether anything happens to Penix or the QB2 during the week. Short of that, Rush stays on the sideline.

restOfSeason.body: The base case is no meaningful snaps. Penix has held the job since Week 3 and Rush is third in line. The projections below assume he is forced into a start. In that case, expect his career norm more than his September: a quick-game passer with time to throw in the mid-2s, an intended air depth around five yards, and a negative CPOE. The 10.3% interception rate and the 62.5% pressure-to-sack rate should both regress toward his history, because both rest on tiny samples and run against what he has done for years. The accuracy deficit and the struggles on longer third downs will not go away, because they are who he has always been.
swingFactors: Health of Penix and the QB2
Whether a start comes against a soft pass defense or a top unit like Minnesota
How much of the offense runs through Bijan Robinson and quick throws

confidence.note: Two games and 46 dropbacks, and he is now QB3 with an uncertain path to playing time.
